claim: An improved 28 GHz microstrip patch antenna using a Roger RT5880LZ substrate and a U-shaped parasitic ground-plane element achieves a return loss of -21.4 dB and gain of 8.19 dBi.
stance_target: feasibility of compact high-gain microstrip patch antennas for 28 GHz 5G mmWave applications
scope_conditions: CST Microwave Studio simulation, not physically fabricated/measured
quoted_support: The proposed MPA has a return loss of -21.4 dB, resonating at the desired resonant frequency of 28 GHz and covering a frequency band of 27.185 GHz – 29.211 GHz with a bandwidth of 2.026 GHz.

claim: Adding a U-shaped parasitic element to the ground plane of a microstrip patch antenna improves gain and bandwidth relative to conventional patch designs without such an element.
stance_target: ground-plane defect/parasitic-element techniques as a low-cost antenna performance enhancement method for student projects
quoted_support: The proposed antenna exhibits a performance improvement in terms of gain and bandwidth due to the addition of U-shaped element when benchmarked with existing designs in the literature work.

claim: The 28 GHz band is preferred among mmWave 5G bands due to lower atmospheric absorption/attenuation compared with other mmWave frequencies.
stance_target: 28 GHz as a practical target frequency for student mmWave antenna projects
quoted_support: Among the existing millimeter waves spectrum, 28-GHz is notably preferred for 5G applications due to its lower atmospheric absorptions and attenuations rates.

claim: The proposed 28 GHz antenna outperforms several previously published 28 GHz microstrip antenna designs on bandwidth and gain simultaneously (Gaid et al. 2024: -45 dB/1.43 GHz/8.1 dB; Farahat & Hussein 2022: -34.5 dB/1.23 GHz/6.6 dB; Raheel et al. 2021: -25 dB/1 GHz/7.1 dB).
stance_target: comparative superiority of the proposed antenna design over prior published designs
scope_conditions: simulation-based comparison table, not independently verified
quoted_support: From the table, the proposed 5G antenna is found to perform better than the majority of the counterparts in terms of the bandwidth and gain.
